claims.text: The investigated FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are initially solid.
Element-specific surface segregation occurs in FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Enhanced surface segregation drives formation of a disordered, liquid-like surface layer.
A liquid-like surface layer forms below the bulk melting point.
Surface premelting reduces the effective melting-onset temperature and alters the overall phase-transition behavior.
Controlled surface treatments or deposited layers can be used to enhance or suppress element-specific segregation.
Preferential segregation of Cu may contribute to formation of the proposed surface layer because Cu has relatively low cohesive energy.
Element-specific segregation reduces the cohesive energy of the nanoparticle surface.
Reduced surface cohesive energy initiates localized surface melting.
Localized surface melting promotes propagation of a melting front into the nanoparticle bulk.
Propagation of the surface-initiated melting front lowers the observable phase-transition temperature relative to unmodified particles.
Particles treated to promote segregation will show an earlier onset of surface melting than unmodified particles.
Particles treated to promote segregation will have a lower overall melting-onset temperature than unmodified particles.
Unmodified nanoparticles will show a higher melting-onset temperature and less pronounced premelting than segregation-promoting particles.
Heating and cooling protocol can affect composition, structure, or phase stability in multielement alloys and nanoparticles.
Holding heating rate and atmosphere constant is intended to isolate the effect of surface-composition modification.
The appearance of a disordered surface layer and the melting-onset temperature can be monitored using in situ high-resolution TEM and calorimetry.
A lack of statistically significant transition differences among segregation-promoting, segregation-suppressing, and unmodified particles would falsify the proposed governing role of segregation.
